text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: Somewhere in Virginia, a company wants to build a data centre. It has the land, the power contract and the investors. And it has a problem that most people never think about. A data centre needs backup power, and backup power usually means a field of large diesel or gas generators. Generators burn fuel. Burning fuel produces air pollution. And before you can install them, you need an air permit.

speaker: JAMES
text: And that permit isn't a form you fill out over lunch. It can mean calculating emissions from every unit, modelling how pollution disperses over the neighbourhood, checking federal, state and local rules, negotiating with regulators and then living with a stack of conditions for as long as the facility runs. Get it wrong and the project slips by months. Or worse, the facility is out of compliance once it's operating.

speaker: NORA
text: The people who do that work are environmental consultants. And today's company is one of the firms that specialises in exactly that, while the software companies circle, armed with AI. Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Today it's ALL4, an environmental consulting firm from Pennsylvania focused on air permitting, compliance and environmental, health and safety support for industrial clients.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: ALL4's own news releases and website, the private equity firm's pages, trade rankings and market research summaries. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a figure comes from the company, a vendor or a research aggregator, we'll flag it. And nothing here is legal, regulatory or investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: And a quick note on the name. It's ALL4, the word "all" and the number four.

speaker: NORA
text: So, the one-sentence version.

speaker: JAMES
text: ALL4 helps industrial companies get the environmental permits they need and stay compliant once they have them, especially on air quality, across energy, manufacturing, data centres, chemicals and pharmaceuticals. It says it has more than four hundred professionals.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting right now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because 2026 has been a very busy year. Three acquisitions in eight months. Two partnerships with environmental software companies, both of which market AI. A security certification. New senior roles. And all of it happening while software vendors are building AI that does some of what consultants bill for by the hour. ALL4 is, in my view, living the central question for professional services firms: do you get squeezed by software, or do you join it?

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the basics. Where is it, when was it founded, who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: ALL4 was founded in 2002 by two childhood friends and their mentors, according to its own site. Headquarters is in Kimberton, Pennsylvania, a small community in Chester County, west of Philadelphia. The private equity firm's page lists Philadelphia, which is presumably shorthand for the region. The firm's own pages give the Kimberton address.

speaker: NORA
text: And the leadership?

speaker: JAMES
text: The chief executive is Bill Straub. One of the co-founders continues to lead the firm alongside him. Ali Farnoud is chief strategy officer. In August 2026 the firm created a new senior role called Principal and named its first three: Sharon Sadler, who focuses on data centres and healthcare, Dan Dix on power generation and data centres, and Eric Libolt on petroleum and refining and remediation.

speaker: NORA
text: What does creating a Principal role tell you?

speaker: JAMES
text: In consulting firms, titles like that usually mark the senior experts who own client relationships and lead a sector. Creating the role for the first time in 2026, after twenty-four years, suggests the firm is formalising its senior structure as it grows, partly, in our inference, to give acquired leaders and home-grown experts a clear path. It's a sign of a firm moving from founder-led to institution-led.

speaker: NORA
text: Data centres appear twice in that list.

speaker: JAMES
text: They do, and that's not an accident. We'll come back to it. There's also Mike Myers, who leads what ALL4 calls its Digital Solutions practice, and in March 2026 it formalised an acoustics practice, with Buddy Ledger as director. Acoustics, meaning noise. Industrial facilities have to manage noise as well as air emissions.

speaker: NORA
text: Size?

speaker: JAMES
text: More than four hundred professionals, by its own count, and it says "and growing." Revenue isn't public. It has offices in California, Georgia, Kentucky, Massachusetts, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, the Virginia and Washington D.C. area, and Washington State, plus an office in Madrid, Spain, and remote staff in Brazil, Canada, Chile and Mexico.

speaker: NORA
text: Madrid is a surprise.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a small international footprint for a firm that's overwhelmingly American in focus. We don't know much about what the Madrid office does, so I won't speculate beyond saying it exists.

speaker: NORA
text: And how is it ranked?

speaker: JAMES
text: In October 2026, it was ranked number one hundred and fifty-five in the Engineering News-Record list of the top two hundred environmental firms, up four places. In June 2026 it was named a Hot Firm by Zweig Group, which tracks architecture, engineering and environmental firms. And in 2024, an independent research firm called Verdantix placed ALL4 as the only "Innovator" among nine providers in its assessment of environmental services. We couldn't see the other names in that report.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the history and ownership.

speaker: JAMES
text: Founded in 2002. Before Levine Leichtman, ALL4 was backed by JMH Capital Partners. And under that earlier owner it was already acquiring firms. In September 2020, Smith Management Group in Kentucky. In October 2020, Environmental Strategy Consultants in Philadelphia. In February 2021, Env Holding Corp in Rancho Cucamonga, California. In January 2024, Whatcom Environmental Services in Bellingham, Washington. And in June 2024, Capaccio Environmental Engineering in New England.

speaker: NORA
text: So a buy-and-build story before the current owner arrived.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very much. Then on the twenty-third of January 2025, Levine Leichtman acquired ALL4 from JMH Capital, in partnership with management. Terms weren't disclosed. The co-founders and the executive team kept significant equity. It was an investment from the firm's Fund VII.

speaker: NORA
text: And since then?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three acquisitions in 2026 alone. In January, VCS Environmental, based in San Juan Capistrano, California, which does work under the California Environmental Quality Act and its federal cousin, the National Environmental Policy Act, plus wetlands and cultural resources. Its chief executive is Julie Beeman. In February, Tora Consulting, from Columbia, South Carolina, whose founder Brandon Mogan, a professional engineer, became president. And in September, Koogler and Associates from Gainesville, Florida, which ALL4 described as one of Florida's longest-established air quality consulting teams. Koogler does air permitting, testing and assessments of continuous emissions monitoring systems, and wastewater work.

speaker: NORA
text: Interesting that the private equity firm's own page doesn't list those.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. The portfolio page shows no add-ons, but ALL4's own news pages announce all three. That's a small inconsistency in public data, nothing more.

speaker: NORA
text: What does it actually take to integrate a consulting firm you've bought?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, more than people expect. You're buying people and relationships, not machines. The founder of the acquired firm usually has the client relationships, so keeping them engaged matters enormously. Then there's the practical layer: moving everyone onto one timekeeping and billing system, one project management approach, one email and document system, common quality review steps, and common templates for reports. And there's culture. A thirty-person regional firm where everyone knows each other doesn't automatically feel at home in a firm of four hundred.

speaker: NORA
text: And the reason to do it anyway?

speaker: JAMES
text: Clients and cross-selling. If Koogler's Florida air quality clients also need remediation or acoustics work, ALL4 can now offer it. And for multi-site clients, one firm across many states is easier to manage than five local ones. That's the theory of the buy-and-build. Whether it works depends on how well the integration is done.

speaker: NORA
text: How long has the current owner held it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Just under two years. So we're early. This is the build phase. Buy firms, add geography and capability, integrate them, then show a bigger, more valuable platform.

speaker: NORA
text: And the pattern of the 2026 deals?

speaker: JAMES
text: Each adds a region and a specialism. California for environmental review. South Carolina for engineering and compliance. Florida for air quality and emissions monitoring. In my view it's a sensible pattern for a firm whose clients often have facilities in many states. A multi-site manufacturer wants one consultant who knows the rules in each state.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the customer's problem. Explain air permitting for someone who's never thought about it.

speaker: JAMES
text: In the US, as general background, the Clean Air Act gives the Environmental Protection Agency and the states the power to regulate air pollution from facilities. If you want to build or significantly change a facility that emits pollutants, a power plant, a refinery, a chemical plant, a factory, a data centre with large generators, you usually need a permit before construction. Then many larger facilities need an operating permit that sets out every limit, every monitoring requirement, every record they must keep and every report they must file.

speaker: NORA
text: And those permits are complicated.

speaker: JAMES
text: Hugely. A major facility's operating permit can run to hundreds of pages, with conditions drawn from federal rules, state rules and sometimes local rules, each with its own monitoring and reporting schedule. Miss a deadline or a calculation and you may have a violation. Violations can mean fines, enforcement and reputational damage.

speaker: NORA
text: How long has this regime been around?

speaker: JAMES
text: The modern Clean Air Act dates from 1970, with major amendments in 1990 that, among other things, created the federal operating permit programme for larger sources, usually called Title V. That's general background. The point is that it's a mature, layered system. Decades of federal rules, plus state implementation plans, plus local air districts, especially in places like California. Each layer adds requirements, and they don't always line up neatly.

speaker: NORA
text: Which is why you need specialists.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Knowing where to look, and how a regulator in a particular state tends to interpret a rule, is the kind of knowledge that sits in experienced people's heads. And that's both ALL4's value and, in a sense, its vulnerability, because AI is getting better at finding and reading rules.

speaker: NORA
text: So the client needs expertise they don't have in-house.

speaker: JAMES
text: Or don't have enough of. Many industrial companies have environmental, health and safety staff, usually shortened to EHS. But they're stretched thin, and permitting is specialised. So they bring in consultants. ALL4 describes itself as becoming "part of their environmental teams," either at a single site or at the corporate level.

speaker: NORA
text: And it's not only air.

speaker: JAMES
text: No. There's compliance support, environmental planning, programme support across health and safety, chemical management, environmental review for new projects in California and elsewhere, remediation of contaminated sites, emissions testing, wastewater and now acoustics. But air quality is the core identity.

speaker: NORA
text: Why is demand rising?

speaker: JAMES
text: Two drivers stand out. First, regulatory churn. ALL4 publishes a regular regulatory roundup. In October 2026 it covered California's climate disclosure law known as Senate Bill 253, new EPA designations for fine particulate pollution, called PM two point five, extended producer responsibility laws for packaging, a proposed EPA rule for gasoline distribution terminals, and California's changes to cancer-risk values for two chemicals, acrolein and ethylene oxide.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a lot in one month.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and every one of those generates work for someone: interpreting the rule, figuring out who it applies to, recalculating, reporting. Second, the build-out of data centres and power generation. That's why ALL4 made those sectors a principal focus.

speaker: NORA
text: Why do data centres need so much environmental work?

speaker: JAMES
text: Our inference on the permit type, based on general knowledge: large data centres often install many backup generators, sometimes dozens, to keep running if the grid fails. Each one is a source of emissions. Some data centres also build on-site power plants. Collectively that can make them significant sources that need air permits. And they're being built at enormous speed, so there's pressure to get permits quickly and right the first time.

speaker: NORA
text: What does an ALL4 engagement actually look like?

speaker: JAMES
text: Think of two broad types. Project work, like getting a permit for a new facility or an expansion. And ongoing compliance support, where ALL4 people are effectively embedded with the client's environmental team, helping them meet their reporting deadlines, calculate emissions and prepare for inspections.

speaker: NORA
text: And who does the work?

speaker: JAMES
text: Engineers and scientists. Air quality specialists, people who do dispersion modelling, which is the maths of how pollution spreads from a stack into the surrounding area, people who know the regulations in detail, and people who manage the client relationship. It's skilled, technical, billable work.

speaker: NORA
text: Tell me more about the quality side. How does a firm like this avoid mistakes?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general practice in engineering consulting, through layers of review. A junior engineer prepares calculations, a more senior person checks them, and a principal or project manager signs off on the final deliverable. Templates and checklists help make sure nothing is missed. And for many submissions, a licensed professional engineer takes responsibility for the technical content.

speaker: NORA
text: That sounds expensive.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and it's also where much of the value lies. A permit application that's wrong can cost a client months. So clients are paying for confidence, not just for pages. That's important for the AI discussion, because AI can produce pages very cheaply. What it can't yet do on its own is give a regulator and a client confidence that the pages are right.

speaker: NORA
text: Billable by the hour?

speaker: JAMES
text: Much of it, in our inference. Public material doesn't describe a proprietary AI product or a big software revenue line, so growth largely tracks the number of skilled people billing time. That's typical for consulting.

speaker: NORA
text: But there's a digital side too.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. The Digital Solutions practice, led by Mike Myers. And when ALL4 acquired Capaccio in 2024, it brought in a product called EHS-Dashboard, a proprietary platform for managing environmental, health and safety information. So there's some software and data capability inside the firm, though it's not AI-specific.

speaker: NORA
text: And the security certification?

speaker: JAMES
text: In December 2025, ALL4 announced certification under ISO/IEC 27001, the international standard for information security management, issued on the first of November 2025. It also launched a public Trust Center, a web page describing its security practices.

speaker: NORA
text: Why would a consultancy bother?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because its clients are energy companies, chemical plants, pharma manufacturers and data centre operators. They're handing over sensitive operating data: production volumes, emissions data, process details. Large clients run serious vendor security reviews. A recognised certification makes those easier. And in my view it's a precondition for any AI workflow that touches client data. If you want to put a client's permit and emissions data through an AI tool, you'd better be able to show you handle data properly.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is the market?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'm going to be careful here, because the estimates are all over the place. One aggregator, SNS Insider, sizes the broad environmental consulting market at about forty-four billion dollars in 2025, forecast to reach about seventy-five billion by 2035, growing just under six percent a year. North America is about a third of that.

speaker: NORA
text: And others?

speaker: JAMES
text: Verdantix, the research firm, put environmental, health and safety services at about forty-three billion dollars in 2023, rising to sixty-three billion by 2029. MarketsandMarkets put the EHS market, software plus services, at about eight billion dollars in 2024. Those two EHS estimates differ by about five times, probably because they define the market differently. So I wouldn't use any of these as a precise number.

speaker: NORA
text: What can we say?

speaker: JAMES
text: That the estimates cluster around six to eight percent annual growth. That's steady, not explosive. So, in our view, a firm like ALL4 grows faster than the market mainly by winning share and buying other firms.

speaker: NORA
text: Who buys?

speaker: JAMES
text: According to that SNS Insider summary, large enterprises are just under half of clients, energy and utilities is the largest end market at about a quarter, and environmental impact assessment is the largest service type. Around fifty-five percent of work is delivered on-site. Government clients are described as the fastest-growing segment. Again, aggregator numbers, so directional.

speaker: NORA
text: Give me a sense of the clients by sector. What does each one need?

speaker: JAMES
text: In broad terms, and this is general background rather than ALL4's client list. Power plants and refineries are large, complex sources with big operating permits and lots of monitoring. Chemical and pharmaceutical plants handle hazardous substances, so chemical management and risk assessments matter. Manufacturers often have many mid-sized sites, each with its own permit and reporting. And data centres are the newcomers: fast-moving developers who may have limited in-house environmental staff and very tight deadlines.

speaker: NORA
text: So different clients buy different things.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. The refinery may want an embedded team for years. The data centre developer may want one permit, fast, then a light-touch compliance programme. A firm that serves both needs flexible ways to price and staff the work.

speaker: NORA
text: And the risk to demand?

speaker: JAMES
text: Regulation can reverse. Some of the 2026 rule churn could be rolled back, which would cut project demand. That's our inference, and it cuts both ways. Even rollbacks generate work, because clients need to know what changed. But a lighter regulatory environment overall would mean less work.

speaker: NORA
text: Who does ALL4 compete with?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a fragmented market of consulting firms, from giant engineering companies to small regional specialists. But in our research, only one consulting competitor came with a usable source: Vanguard Environmental, a private firm founded in 1992, which sells compliance work at flat-rate fees and claims more North American clients than any rival. That's its claim.

speaker: NORA
text: Flat-rate fees. Interesting.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, because it's a different commercial model from billing by the hour. If a competitor offers a fixed price for a compliance programme, and uses technology to deliver it efficiently, that's pricing pressure on hourly firms.

speaker: NORA
text: And the software side?

speaker: JAMES
text: This is where it gets interesting. There are software companies selling AI-embedded compliance tools. Encamp has a compliance platform with an AI agent called Scout that identifies which regulatory duties apply to a facility and checks data against federal, state and local rules. Benchmark Gensuite, based in Mason, Ohio, sells an environmental management suite covering air, refrigerants, waste, permits and water, with an embedded assistant called Genny AI. VelocityEHS sells a platform called Accelerate, which it markets as AI-powered. And EcoOnline sells EHS and chemical management software called EcoOne, with what it calls embedded AI.

speaker: NORA
text: And two of those are now partners.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. In September 2026, ALL4 and VelocityEHS announced a partnership pairing the Accelerate platform with ALL4's consulting. VelocityEHS's material talks about having PhD AI and machine learning scientists on its side. Then in October 2026, ALL4 and EcoOnline formed an alliance, with ALL4 becoming an implementation partner and advisor for EcoOne.

speaker: NORA
text: Two software alliances in five weeks.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a strategic signal. In my view, ALL4 is positioning itself as the expert layer on top of software platforms. The client buys the software. ALL4 configures it, connects it to the client's real permits and processes, advises on the regulatory content and helps the client's staff use it.

speaker: NORA
text: What does implementation work actually involve?

speaker: JAMES
text: Imagine a manufacturer with twenty plants buys an EHS software platform. Someone has to load every permit and its conditions into the system, set up the tasks and deadlines, connect it to the plants' data on emissions, chemicals and incidents, configure the reports for each state, and train the staff at each plant. The software vendor knows the software. The consultant knows the regulations and the client's facilities. Done badly, the client ends up with an expensive system nobody trusts. Done well, it becomes the backbone of their compliance programme.

speaker: NORA
text: And that work is billable too.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very much. And it tends to lead to ongoing work: updates when rules change, audits, support. So the alliances could turn into a steady stream of revenue for ALL4, if clients actually buy the platforms through it.

speaker: NORA
text: But aren't those vendors also competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: They can be. Software vendors often have their own implementation and advisory staff. And if the software gets good enough at identifying duties and checking compliance automatically, the client may need less consulting. So these are partners today and potential competitors tomorrow. It's what people sometimes call co-opetition.

speaker: NORA
text: So which way does it go?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the big question. My view is that the software will automate the routine parts of compliance: tracking deadlines, collecting data, flagging gaps. The judgement-heavy parts, like interpreting an ambiguous rule, negotiating with a regulator or designing a permit strategy for a new facility, stay human for a good while. The firms that win will be the ones that let software do the routine work and charge for judgement.

speaker: NORA
text: So where is ALL4 itself with AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's be precise. The earliest piece of evidence is from November 2021, when ALL4 announced a partnership with ehsAI, an AI platform that turns permit documents into compliance requirement lists. ALL4 said it would use ehsAI to strengthen its compliance services. That's a real and quite early AI move for a consultancy.

speaker: NORA
text: And since then?

speaker: JAMES
text: The 2026 alliances, with VelocityEHS and EcoOnline, both cite AI. But the AI belongs to the partners' products. ALL4 provides the advisory and implementation. We didn't find an ALL4-built AI product, an AI-titled leadership role or a published AI budget.

speaker: NORA
text: And governance?

speaker: JAMES
text: The ISO 27001 certification and the Trust Center are about information security generally. We didn't find an AI-specific policy, an AI governance body or anything describing how ALL4 uses AI on client data. For a firm handling sensitive industrial data, that would be a good next step.

speaker: NORA
text: Are clients asking for AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't have direct evidence of what ALL4's clients are asking. But the trend is visible in the market: Encamp, Benchmark Gensuite, EcoOnline and VelocityEHS all now sell embedded AI for permit and compliance tasks. So any client evaluating EHS software in 2026 is seeing AI in the demos. In our view, that raises the client's expectations of their consultant too. If the software can draft a compliance calendar in minutes, why should the consultant take two weeks?

speaker: NORA
text: That's an uncomfortable question for a consultant.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. And the honest answer has to be, "we'll use those tools too, and we'll spend our time on the part that actually needs an expert."

speaker: NORA
text: And the digital practice?

speaker: JAMES
text: The Digital Solutions practice and the EHS-Dashboard product show genuine technology capability. They're the natural home for AI work. But we don't have public evidence of AI inside ALL4's core delivery today, beyond the 2021 plan.

speaker: NORA
text: So your overall read?

speaker: JAMES
text: ALL4 is thoughtful and early on the strategy. It saw permit-to-requirement extraction as an AI use case back in 2021. It's chosen a partnering strategy with software vendors. It has security credentials in place. What's missing, publicly, is evidence of AI changing how its own people deliver work day to day. That's the next chapter.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make it concrete. Walk me through an engagement. Invented, not real.

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's say a developer is building a data centre campus in the Southeast. Call the developer Bluewater. The campus will have forty backup diesel generators. Bluewater hires ALL4 to get the air permit and then help it stay compliant.

speaker: NORA
text: What happens first?

speaker: JAMES
text: A senior consultant, call him Raj, meets the client. He gathers the details: the generator models, their size, how often they'll be tested, the fuel, the site layout, the stack heights. Then a junior engineer, call her Emma, calculates the potential emissions of each pollutant from each unit, using manufacturer data and emission factors.

speaker: NORA
text: And then the modelling?

speaker: JAMES
text: If needed, a modeller runs a dispersion model to estimate concentrations at the property boundary and in the neighbourhood, and compares them with air quality standards. Meanwhile Raj works out which rules apply. Federal standards for those engines, the state's permitting rules, any local requirements, and whether the total emissions push the facility into a bigger permitting category.

speaker: NORA
text: And then they write it up.

speaker: JAMES
text: Emma drafts the application. It's a long document: a description of the project, emission calculations, the regulatory analysis, the modelling results, proposed permit conditions. Raj reviews it, sends comments, Emma revises. A principal does a final quality review. That drafting and review cycle might take weeks.

speaker: NORA
text: And then the regulator.

speaker: JAMES
text: The application goes to the state agency. The agency asks questions. ALL4 responds. Eventually a permit is issued, often with conditions: limits on testing hours, monitoring, record-keeping, reports.

speaker: NORA
text: And then compliance.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. Now someone has to turn that permit into a list of obligations. Every condition, who's responsible, what records to keep, what reports are due and when. Then, every month, someone collects the generator run hours and fuel use, checks them against the limits and prepares the reports.

speaker: NORA
text: Where does AI fit?

speaker: JAMES
text: In several places. First, extracting the requirements from the permit into a structured compliance table, which is exactly what ehsAI was built for. Hours of careful reading become minutes of review. Second, drafting the narrative sections of the application from the engineering inputs and the firm's past applications, so Emma starts from a decent first draft. Third, checking the regulatory analysis against a database of rules, which is what tools like Encamp's Scout claim to do. And fourth, on the compliance side, flagging when run hours are trending toward a limit before it's exceeded.

speaker: NORA
text: What stays human?

speaker: JAMES
text: The judgement. Whether to accept a permit limit or negotiate it. How to design testing schedules to give the client flexibility. How to talk to the regulator. And the professional responsibility for what's submitted. An AI draft doesn't sign a permit application. A qualified person does.

speaker: NORA
text: And what changes for Bluewater?

speaker: JAMES
text: If done well, faster permits, fewer revisions and a cleaner compliance programme from day one. For a data centre developer under time pressure, speed to permit is worth a lot.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk challenges.

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, the billable-hour model. If AI makes the drafting and extraction work much faster, and ALL4 bills by the hour, revenue per project could fall. That's the classic professional services dilemma.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Integration. Three acquisitions in eight months across California, South Carolina and Florida, on top of five earlier ones. Each firm brings its own people, clients, culture and, often, its own systems: timekeeping, project management, document storage, templates. That's our inference, but it's typical. AI needs consistent data and templates, and integration comes first.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a capacity challenge with the data centre boom?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd think so, in our inference. If many developers want permits at the same time, the bottleneck is the number of experienced air permitting specialists, both at consultancies and at state agencies. A firm can't hire senior experts overnight. That's actually one of the strongest arguments for AI at ALL4: not to cut people, but to let the experts it has handle more projects without quality slipping.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Leadership is still forming. The Principal role was only created in August 2026. Founders still lead. That's not bad, but it means decision rights and succession are still being set. That's our inference.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Talent. Growth depends on a fairly small senior bench of technical experts who know the regulations deeply. They're hard to hire and easy to lose. And if junior work gets automated, there's a longer-term question about how the next generation of experts learns.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: The software squeeze. Partners like VelocityEHS and EcoOnline are friends today. But if they automate more and offer their own advisory services, they could take work from consultants. And flat-fee competitors like Vanguard put pressure on pricing.

speaker: NORA
text: And the people inside ALL4. How do engineers feel about AI drafting their work?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't have any public evidence on that specifically, so this is general. In professional firms, there are usually three reactions. Some people are enthusiastic early adopters. Some are sceptical, often the most senior experts, who've seen tools over-promise and who know how subtle the regulations can be. And some are quietly worried about what it means for their jobs. Leaders have to address all three.

speaker: NORA
text: How?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, by starting with the tasks nobody enjoys, like transcribing permit conditions into spreadsheets, by letting the sceptical experts test the tools and find the errors, and by being honest about how efficiency gains will be used. If the message is "we'll take on more data centre work without burning everyone out," that's a very different story from "we'll need fewer of you."

speaker: NORA
text: That learning question is interesting. If Emma doesn't spend weeks drafting applications, how does she become Raj?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a real issue across all professional services. My view is that firms will have to design training deliberately, with juniors reviewing and critiquing AI drafts, learning why a calculation is right, rather than learning purely by repetition. Done well, they might learn faster. Done badly, they'll learn less.

speaker: NORA
text: Opportunities.

speaker: JAMES
text: The first is generative AI for permit and regulatory extraction. Turning permits and new rules into compliance requirement tables. ALL4 identified this in 2021 with ehsAI, and the regulatory churn of 2026 makes it more valuable. The payoff is in labour hours in the air and permitting practice.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Automated emissions and continuous monitoring reporting. Koogler brings expertise in continuous emissions monitoring systems and air testing. AI could draft and quality-check those reports, cutting senior review hours. Our inference.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Implementation revenue from the software alliances. Selling configuration, data migration and change management for EcoOne and Accelerate. That raises revenue per client and moves ALL4 toward recurring work.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: The data centre and power vertical. Air permits for backup generators and turbines are a repeatable need, our inference on the permit type, and ALL4 has two principals focused on it. Repeatable work is exactly where AI templates and drafting tools pay off.

speaker: NORA
text: Others?

speaker: JAMES
text: Remediation and petroleum and refining work, which is Eric Libolt's focus, with potential cross-selling across the Gulf and Texas footprint. A recurring compliance subscription, converting one-off permit projects into managed monitoring contracts, which the software partners can support. And more bolt-on acquisitions in air quality or environmental review, following the VCS and Koogler pattern.

speaker: NORA
text: What about government clients? You said they were the fastest-growing segment.

speaker: JAMES
text: In that aggregator's summary, yes. VCS Environmental's work on California and federal environmental review is the kind of capability that public agencies and infrastructure projects need, since environmental review applies to many public projects as well as private ones. We don't know how much of ALL4's work is for government today. But if that segment really is growing fastest, VCS gives ALL4 a foothold, and environmental review documents are long, structured and repetitive, which is again fertile ground for AI drafting.

speaker: NORA
text: And the acoustics practice?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a nice example of cross-selling. A data centre with dozens of generators and cooling equipment can be loud, and neighbours notice. Noise studies are often part of local approvals. If ALL4 is already doing the air permit, offering the noise study too is natural. Small practices like that make the firm stickier with clients.

speaker: NORA
text: The subscription one sounds important.

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view it's the strategic answer to the billable-hour dilemma. If ALL4 sells "we'll keep your facility compliant for a fixed monthly fee," using software and AI to deliver it efficiently, then efficiency becomes margin rather than lost revenue. It's how a services firm becomes a services-plus-software firm.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do a second walk-through. A new regulation lands. Invented again.

speaker: JAMES
text: Say a pharmaceutical manufacturer in California, call it Coastline Pharma, uses ethylene oxide to sterilise medical products. California changes the cancer-risk value for ethylene oxide, which is one of the changes ALL4's October roundup mentioned. Coastline's environmental manager, call her Priya, emails ALL4: what does this mean for us?

speaker: NORA
text: And today, how does ALL4 answer?

speaker: JAMES
text: A consultant reads the new value and the agency guidance, pulls Coastline's existing risk assessment and permit, works out which calculations change, reruns the risk numbers, and writes a memo. Then multiply that by every client that uses ethylene oxide or acrolein. Each one gets a careful but largely manual analysis.

speaker: NORA
text: And with AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: The firm's tools would identify every client whose permits or inventories mention those chemicals within hours of the change. For each, AI pulls the relevant permit conditions and past assessments, and drafts a first impact summary: here's what changed, here's which of your calculations are affected, here's the rough direction of the result. The consultant checks the numbers, adds judgement about what the agency is likely to do next, and sends it.

speaker: NORA
text: So ALL4 calls Priya before she calls ALL4.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. That's the shift from reactive to proactive. And it's a sales opportunity too. "Here's what the new rule means for you, and here's what we suggest" is a very good conversation starter for the next project.

speaker: NORA
text: What could go wrong?

speaker: JAMES
text: The AI could miss a client, misread an older permit, or get a calculation wrong. In a health-risk context, that's serious. So the human check isn't optional. And the client data has to be organised well enough to be searched in the first place, which brings us back to integration.

speaker: NORA
text: If you had to pick one AI bet for the next eighteen months?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Permit and regulatory requirement extraction, plus draft report generation, for the air quality and compliance practice. It's the core of the business, the work is document-heavy and repeatable, ALL4 has already chosen this direction, and the security certification gives it a foundation to handle client data.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: How would you run the first hundred days?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: pick one practice area, say air permitting for generators and turbines, where the work is most repeatable. Choose a small team of volunteers across two or three offices, ideally including people from an acquired firm. Collect a library of past permits, applications and compliance tables, with client permission where needed. Agree the measures: hours to produce a compliance table, hours to first draft of an application, number of review comments, and error rates.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Days thirty to sixty?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Run AI extraction and drafting on real projects in parallel with the normal process. Every output is reviewed by a qualified engineer. Track where the AI gets it wrong. Is it misreading a condition? Missing a cross-reference to a federal rule? That error log is gold.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And sixty to a hundred?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Compare hours and quality. If the drafts are good and the hours fall, standardise templates across offices, including the acquired firms, and decide how to price. Do you keep billing hourly and accept lower revenue per project, offer fixed-fee permit packages, or bundle it into a compliance subscription? Make that commercial decision deliberately, based on evidence, rather than letting it happen by default.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: What about the data itself? Can ALL4 use one client's permits to help another?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a sensitive question, and I'd treat it carefully. Many permits are public records, filed with regulators, so in principle a library built from public permits is fair game. But a client's internal emissions data, process details and draft applications are confidential. So the safe design, in my view, is a library built from public documents and the firm's own templates, with each client's confidential data used only for that client's work, unless contracts explicitly say otherwise.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And governance?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Write and publish an AI use policy alongside the Trust Center. Which tools are approved, how client data is handled, whether data is used to train models, and the rule that a qualified human reviews and signs everything. Clients in energy and pharma will ask, so answer the question before they do.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Who owns it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: One person with both technical credibility and authority. The Digital Solutions practice is a natural home, paired with a principal from the air practice, but with one accountable owner.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: What can other businesses learn from ALL4?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four lessons. First, if software is coming for your work, partner with it before it competes with you. ALL4's two alliances are a bet that the expert layer on top of software is valuable. Whether that bet works depends on execution, but it's better than pretending the software doesn't exist.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Decide your pricing model before AI decides it for you. If AI cuts the hours, an hourly firm either gets more work done for the same revenue, or less revenue for the same work. Fixed fees and subscriptions turn efficiency into margin. That's a choice to make deliberately.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Security first, then AI. The ISO certification came before the AI push. In industries with sensitive data, that's the right order.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Integrate acquisitions into one way of working, or AI won't scale. Templates, document libraries, timekeeping, project codes. A roll-up of eight consulting firms with eight ways of writing a permit application can't use one AI drafting tool well.

speaker: NORA
text: Anything about the data centre focus that generalises?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. Follow the build-out. When a whole industry is building at speed, it creates repeatable, urgent work, and repeatable work is exactly where templates and AI tools pay off first. ALL4 created principals around data centres and power. Other services firms should ask where their clients are building fastest, and design their AI around that work.

speaker: NORA
text: And I'd add a fifth: train the next generation on purpose.

speaker: JAMES
text: Agreed. If AI does the first draft, make sure juniors learn to judge drafts, not just to accept them.

speaker: NORA
text: One more lesson. What about being early?

speaker: JAMES
text: Being early on an idea isn't the same as being early on adoption. ALL4 announced its ehsAI partnership in 2021, well ahead of the generative AI wave. That's foresight. But five years later, the public evidence of AI in everyday delivery is still thin. The lesson, in my view, is that the idea is the easy part. The hard part is getting it into the daily work of hundreds of engineers across many offices. Any company that announced an AI partnership a few years ago should ask honestly how much it changed the work.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a fair challenge to a lot of companies.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. And it's not a criticism of ALL4 specifically. We simply can't see inside. It's a question every firm should ask itself.

speaker: NORA
text: Risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, AI disruption to billable hours. Tools like Encamp's and Benchmark Gensuite's automate duty-tracking and data checks that consultants bill for today. Two, software vendors moving into services and taking share. Three, price pressure from flat-fee rivals. Four, regulatory rollback reducing demand. And five, key-person and talent risk in a small senior bench. Most of those are our inferences rather than reported events.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me push back on the first one. Hasn't consulting survived every wave of software so far?

speaker: JAMES
text: It has, and that's a fair challenge. Spreadsheets, databases, EHS software in the 2000s and 2010s. Each time, the routine work shrank and the advisory work grew. Regulation got more complex, which created more work. I think that pattern probably continues. But generative AI is different in one way: it reads and writes text, which is what much of consulting delivers. So the routine slice it can take is bigger than before. The firms that adapt will be fine. The firms that keep billing for transcription won't.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owners?

speaker: JAMES
text: Integration risk. Eight acquisitions in about six years, three in 2026. The value of a buy-and-build comes from the combined platform being worth more than the parts. That only happens if the parts actually work together.

speaker: NORA
text: And when might the owners want to sell?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't know, and nothing has been announced. Private equity holds often run four to seven years, as general background, and this one is under two years old. So the next few years are about building the platform. But a future buyer will look closely at two things, in my view: how much revenue is recurring rather than project-based, and whether the firm has a credible answer to AI. Both are worth working on now.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four things. First, any evidence of AI inside ALL4's own delivery, like an extraction or drafting tool rolled out across the firm. Second, whether the VelocityEHS and EcoOnline alliances produce named client implementations. Third, any shift toward fixed-fee or subscription compliance offerings. And fourth, more acquisitions, and whether they follow the regional air quality pattern.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. ALL4 is a Pennsylvania-based environmental consulting firm, founded in 2002, with more than four hundred professionals, focused on air permitting and compliance for industrial clients including energy, manufacturing, chemicals, pharma and, increasingly, data centres. Levine Leichtman acquired it from JMH Capital in January 2025, and in 2026 alone it bought VCS Environmental, Tora Consulting and Koogler and Associates, signed alliances with VelocityEHS and EcoOnline, created principal roles and earned ISO 27001 certification. On AI, it moved early with ehsAI in 2021, but today the visible AI sits in its partners' software. The opportunity is to use AI for permit extraction and drafting, and to shift toward fixed-fee and subscription work so that efficiency becomes margin.

speaker: JAMES
text: And my closing thought. For a consulting firm, AI isn't just a productivity tool. It's a pricing decision. The firms that decide how to charge for judgement, rather than hours, are the ones that will come out ahead.
